title: Vietnam in Ten Days: A North-to-South Itinerary That Is Not a Race
metaDescription: A realistic ten-day Vietnam itinerary covering Hanoi, Ha Long or Ninh Binh, Hoi An and the south — with transport, costs and what to cut.
excerpt: Vietnam is 1,600 kilometres long. Ten days means choosing two regions properly rather than four badly.
author: Trypinn Team
content:
The standard Vietnam itinerary tries to cover Hanoi, Ha Long Bay, Hue, Hoi An, Ho Chi Minh City and the Mekong Delta in ten days. It is achievable, in the sense that you will physically be in all those places, and it involves four internal flights and a permanent sense of packing.

The better version accepts a simple constraint: **Vietnam is longer than Italy**, and ten days buys you two regions explored properly.

Here is that itinerary, plus the honest guidance on what to cut.

## When to Go

Vietnam's length means there is no single good season — the north and south have different climates entirely.

- **North (Hanoi, Sapa, Ha Long)** — best October to December and March to April. Cold and grey January and February; hot and wet in summer
- **Central (Hue, Hoi An, Da Nang)** — best February to May. Heavy rain and occasional typhoons September to November
- **South (Ho Chi Minh City, Mekong, Phu Quoc)** — dry season December to April
- **The single best overall window** — **February to April**, when all three regions are reasonable simultaneously

Avoid **Tet**, the lunar new year, unless you specifically want to experience it — much of the country closes, transport sells out, and prices rise.

![Vietnam travel](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1441632260885-881646a7fd4d?fm=webp&w=1200&q=60)

## The Ten-Day Itinerary: North and Centre

This is the version most first-time visitors are happiest with.

**Days 1–3: Hanoi**

The best city in Vietnam, and one that rewards wandering more than sightseeing.

- **The Old Quarter** — narrow streets historically organised by trade, still chaotic, best explored on foot with no destination
- **Hoan Kiem Lake** at dawn, when the city exercises
- **The Temple of Literature**, Vietnam's first university
- **Street food** — this is the point. Bun cha for lunch, pho for breakfast, banh mi from a cart, egg coffee in the afternoon, bia hoi on a plastic stool at 5pm
- **The Ho Chi Minh Mausoleum complex** and the Vietnam Museum of Ethnology if you want structured sightseeing

Three days sounds like a lot for one city. It is not. Hanoi is where most people decide they like Vietnam.

**Days 4–5: Ninh Binh or Ha Long Bay**

Choose one. This is the itinerary's main decision.

**Ha Long Bay** is the famous one — limestone karsts rising from the sea, best experienced on an overnight boat. It is also heavily visited and heavily commercialised. If you go, go to **Lan Ha Bay** or **Bai Tu Long** instead, which are the same geology with a fraction of the boats, and book a smaller vessel.

**Ninh Binh** is the inland version — the same karst landscape rising from rice paddies and rivers, often called "Ha Long Bay on land". Cheaper, less crowded, and explored by rowing boat through caves at Trang An and by bicycle between temples. Many travellers now prefer it.

If you have two extra days, **Ha Giang** in the far north is the most spectacular landscape in the country — a mountain loop best done over three or four days, traditionally by motorbike with a driver. It is the single strongest argument for extending a Vietnam trip.

**Day 6: Fly to Da Nang**

Short domestic flight. Internal flights in Vietnam are cheap, frequent and the right choice over the very long train journeys unless the train is the point.

![Vietnam travel](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1570366583862-f91883984fde?fm=webp&w=1200&q=60)

**Days 7–10: Hoi An and Central Vietnam**

**Hoi An** is a preserved trading port of yellow merchant houses, lanterns, tailors and one of the best food scenes in Southeast Asia. It is touristed, unapologetically so, and still lovely — particularly early in the morning and after the day-trippers leave.

- **The old town** at dawn and after dark
- **An Bang beach**, ten minutes away by bicycle
- **A cooking class**, which in Hoi An is genuinely worth doing
- **Tailoring**, if you want something made — allow two days for fittings
- **My Son**, the Cham temple ruins, as a half-day trip
- **The Hai Van Pass** — one of the world's great coastal roads, between Da Nang and Hue, by motorbike with a driver or by car

**Hue**, the imperial capital, is two hours north and holds the Citadel and the royal tombs along the Perfume River. Worth a day trip or an overnight if history interests you; skippable if it does not.

Fly home from Da Nang.

## The Alternative: South and Centre

If you must see Ho Chi Minh City:

- **Days 1–3** — Ho Chi Minh City: the War Remnants Museum, the Reunification Palace, District 1 and the street food, with the Cu Chi tunnels as a half day
- **Day 4** — Mekong Delta overnight, staying in a homestay rather than day-tripping from the city
- **Days 5–6** — fly to Da Nang
- **Days 7–10** — Hoi An and central Vietnam

Ho Chi Minh City is energetic, chaotic and modern. Most travellers prefer Hanoi. Both are worth seeing; neither is worth doing badly in one day.

## What to Cut

Be honest about the arithmetic:

- **Cut Sapa** from a ten-day trip. It is a long way north and needs three days to be worth the journey
- **Cut the Mekong** if you are doing the north — they are at opposite ends of the country
- **Cut Hue** if history is not your priority
- **Do not try to do Hanoi, Hoi An and Ho Chi Minh City plus Ha Long and the Mekong.** That is a fourteen-day trip compressed into ten, and it is mostly airports

## Practicalities

- **Visa** — an e-visa is available to most nationalities, processed online in a few working days. Apply on the **official government portal**; Vietnam has a large ecosystem of lookalike sites charging many times the fee. Check that your stated entry and exit points match your flights
- **Money** — Vietnamese dong. Cash dominates outside cities. Note the number of zeros; confusing 50,000 with 500,000 is a common and expensive mistake
- **Transport** — domestic flights for long hops, Grab for city transport, and a driver rather than self-driving for mountain roads
- **Motorbikes** — the classic way to see the country and the most common cause of serious injury. If you ride, check your insurance covers it and that you hold a licence valid in Vietnam. Many travellers hire a driver instead, which costs little and removes the risk
- **Costs** — budget $25–35 a day, mid-range $50–80, comfortable $120–180. Vietnam remains one of the best-value destinations in Asia

## The Food

Worth its own paragraph, because it is a legitimate reason to choose Vietnam over its neighbours. Pho, bun cha, banh mi, cao lau in Hoi An, bun bo Hue, com tam in the south, fresh spring rolls everywhere, and coffee culture that runs from strong iced ca phe sua da to the egg coffee of Hanoi.

Eat at the plastic-stool places. The best food in Vietnam is on the pavement, and the stall that only sells one dish has been perfecting it for thirty years.

Ten days, two regions, one internal flight. It is less on paper and considerably more in practice — and agreeing that shape with your travel companions before anyone books is the difference between a trip and a transit schedule. Sketching the two-region version and the four-region version side by side in **Trypinn** usually settles the argument quickly, because the travel time becomes visible.
